title: Mid-scan angle progress is lost on process death even though every captured image is still on disk
evidence: `private val _state = MutableStateFlow(ScanState())` plus `private val capturedPaths = mutableMapOf<Angle, String>()`, `qualityResults`, `palmMetricsByAngle` (lines 93-99). No `SavedStateHandle` is injected — grep confirms every `SavedStateHandle` in app/src/main is read-only for nav args, and no ViewModel in the app ever writes to one. Yet the frames are durably persisted: `captureCurrentAngle` writes `File(File(appContext.filesDir, "scans/$monthKey"), "${angle.name}.jpg")` (lines 196-198). The manifest declares no `configChanges` and no `screenOrientation`, and the ScanScreen keeps the camera bound — so a backgrounded scan (phone call, notification tap) is a prime low-memory kill target. PRD line 573 requires "App does not crash on low-memory devices".
fix: Inject `private val savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle` into ScanViewModel (nav-scoped VMs get one whose contents survive process death via the NavBackStackEntry's saved state). Persist a single key, e.g. `savedStateHandle["completedAngles"] = _state.value.completedAngles.map { it.name }.toTypedArray()`, and write it in BOTH places that mutate progress: the success branch at line 259-267 AND retakePreviousAngle (lines 282-295) -- otherwise a stale snapshot plus the still-present file (retake does not delete the jpg) resurrects the very frame the user rejected. Do not bother persisting currentAngleIndex separately; angles are always captured in Angle.entries order, so index == completedAngles.size and deriving it avoids a second key drifting out of sync. Perform the rehydration NOT in init, but at the end of initAnalyzer()'s success path (line 165), after `analyzer` is non-null -- calling analyzeGuarded before that returns null at line 347 and silently restores nothing. Rehydrate by walking Angle.entries in ordinal order, stopping at the first angle that is either absent from the saved set or whose File(appContext.filesDir, "scans/${YearMonth.now()}/${angle.name}.jpg") no longer exists (keeps capturedPaths and the derived index contiguous), and for each surviving frame re-run decodeSampledBitmap + analyzeGuarded + qualityGate.scoreFrame to refill capturedPaths/qualityResults/palmMetricsByAngle, then update _state with the restored completedAngles and index. Skip rehydration entirely if YearMonth.now() no longer matches the month the frames were written under. Clear the key in runPipeline's success branch (line 499). A cheaper alternative that avoids the model-ready dependency: write the per-angle QualityScores and PalmMetrics into the SavedStateHandle (or a small sidecar JSON in the scan dir) at capture time, so restore needs no bitmap decode or analyzer at all.
userImpact: A user 6 of 7 angles into a 90-second capture takes a phone call; Android reclaims the process; they return to "0 / 7" with no explanation, having to redo the whole physically awkward sequence — while the six good photos sit unused on disk.
verifierNote: Confirmed by reading the code. ScanViewModel.kt:93-99 keeps every piece of scan progress in a plain MutableStateFlow plus three plain mutableMapOf's; no SavedStateHandle is injected (grep: only JournalViewModel:25, ResultsViewModel:60, DomainDetailViewModel:33, GuidanceViewModel:39 take one, all read-only nav args). Frames are durably persisted at filesDir/scans/<monthKey>/<ANGLE>.jpg (lines 196-198) and are deleted only on gate failure (line 247) or by ScanImageCleanupWorker after 24h, so the captured images genuinely outlive the process. Nothing restores them: init (line 132) only calls checkAndDownloadModel(), and ScanScreen has no restore path. The report is in fact understated in one respect: ScanScreen.kt:121 keeps `phase` in rememberSaveable, so after process death the screen restores directly into PreScanPhase.CAPTURE while the ViewModel is brand new -- the user lands on CaptureScreen reading 0/7 with up to six valid JPGs on disk. Re-analysis is viable because ImageQualityAnalyzer.analyze is per-frame stateless (stability is the constant 0.9f default), so restored qualityResults/palmMetrics would reproduce exactly. Two things the auditor got wrong. (1) Severity: the PRD line is 569, not 573, and it reads "App does not crash on low-memory devices" -- nothing crashes, nothing is corrupted, and the state is fully recoverable by re-capturing (the next capture of an angle simply overwrites the same filename). (2) The proposed fix is broken as written: rehydrating in init "before checkAndDownloadModel()" calls analyzeGuarded while `analyzer` is still null (it is only assigned in initAnalyzer, which may sit behind an async model download), so analyzeGuarded returns null at line 347 and nothing is restored. title: Application.onCreate forks a `which su` process and blocks on its stdout before the first frame
evidence:
`onCreate()` calls `runSecurityCheck()` synchronously (line 35), which calls `SecurityChecker.check(this)`. Inside `SecurityChecker.checkRoot()` (SecurityChecker.kt:48-70) the main thread performs 8 `File(it).exists()` stats (line 59), one `File("$it/su").exists()` per `PATH` entry (lines 61-62), and then:
```kotlin
val process = Runtime.getRuntime().exec(arrayOf("which", "su"))
process.inputStream.bufferedReader().readLine() != null
```
That is a `fork`/`exec` of a child process plus a blocking `readLine()` on the UI thread. `checkSignature()` (lines 90-108) then adds a `packageManager.getPackageInfo(packageName, GET_SIGNING_CERTIFICATES)` binder call, which parses the APK signing block. Lines 36-37 add a `NotificationManager.createNotificationChannel` binder call and `WorkManager.getInstance(this)` on the same thread. An IO scope already exists at line 27 (`appScope`) and is used for `ensureInstallId()`, so nothing here requires the main thread.

verifierNote: Confirmed by reading both files. title: Capture framing brackets re-record a full-screen display list at 60 fps for the entire scan session

```kotlin
val pulseAlpha by infiniteTransition.animateFloat(
    initialValue = PULSE_MIN_ALPHA, targetValue = PULSE_MAX_ALPHA,
    animationSpec = infiniteRepeatable(
        tween(durationMillis = PULSE_DURATION_MS, easing = FastOutSlowInEasing),
        RepeatMode.Reverse,
    ),
    label = "bracket_pulse",
)
Canvas(modifier = modifier) { drawBrackets(alpha = pulseAlpha) }
```
`pulseAlpha` is read inside the `Canvas` draw lambda, so every animation tick invalidates the draw phase and re-records the layer's display list. `ScanScreen.kt:315` passes `modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize()`, so this is a full-screen node. `PreviewView` runs in its own `SurfaceView` and updates independently of the View hierarchy, so without this animation the Compose window would be idle between captures; with it, the whole overlay window is redrawn continuously for the entire 7-angle capture flow (`PULSE_DURATION_MS = 1000`, `RepeatMode.Reverse`, no stop condition). The alpha is the only thing that changes — the eight `drawLine` geometries are constant.
fix:
The proposed code is correct and compiles against Compose BOM 2024.06.00 (the `graphicsLayer { }` lambda overload the repo already uses at `MotionPreferences.kt:51`). Apply it as written — replace `CaptureFramingOverlay.kt:41-52` with the `PulsingBracketsCanvas` that keeps the animation as a `State<Float>` (no `by`), moves the read into `modifier.graphicsLayer { alpha = pulseAlpha.value }`, and draws at `alpha = 1f`; drop the `androidx.compose.runtime.getValue` import at line 11 and add `androidx.compose.ui.graphics.graphicsLayer`.

1. The benefit is narrower than claimed. This removes the per-tick re-record of the Compose window's display list only. The frame is still scheduled and re-rasterised 60 times a second — `RenderNodeLayer.updateLayerProperties` propagates damage via `onDescendantInvalidated` — so battery, heat, and GPU cost are essentially unchanged. Do not land this expecting a measurable power win; land it as consistency with the existing `graphicsLayer`-alpha pattern used elsewhere in the same package.

2. "the visible alpha range is unchanged" is not exactly true. Each corner's two `drawLine` calls share an endpoint with `StrokeCap.Round`, so today the overlapping corner pixels composite twice (0.4 over 0.4 ≈ 0.64 effective) while layer alpha yields a uniform 0.4. The difference is a few pixels at each of the four corners and is arguably cleaner, but it is a real (if invisible) rendering change, so note it rather than claiming pixel identity.

If the goal is actually to cut power during the capture flow, the higher-leverage change is to the animation itself, not its plumbing — e.g. lengthening `PULSE_DURATION_MS` or dropping the pulse for a static bracket, which is what the `reduceMotion` branch at line 33 already does.
userImpact: The phone keeps re-recording and re-rasterising a full-screen layer 60 times a second for the whole scan — measurable extra battery drain and heat during a flow the user is already holding the camera up for, and the preview is more likely to drop frames on lower-end devices.

The mechanism checks out, but the claimed impact does not survive scrutiny, so this is a low-severity micro-optimization, not a medium perf defect.

VERIFIED: `CaptureFramingOverlay.kt:43` uses `by` delegation, so the `pulseAlpha` read really does happen at its use site inside the `Canvas` draw lambda on line 51 (not during composition). `Canvas` is `Spacer(modifier.drawBehind(onDraw))`, and nothing between it and the Compose root owns a layer — `ScanScreen.kt:310-315` is a plain `Box` with `Modifier.fillMaxSize()`, no `graphicsLayer`, no elevation. So each tick calls `invalidateDraw()`, which walks up to `AndroidComposeView.invalidate()` and re-records the window's display list. `CameraPreview` uses `PreviewView` in default PERFORMANCE mode (SurfaceView on most devices), so it does not itself drive per-frame Compose invalidation; between shutter presses this pulse is the only continuous animation on the screen (`HandOverlay` is fully static, `CircularProgressIndicator` only renders while `isCapturing`, which is exactly when the overlay is hidden via `visible = !isCapturing`). The fix is also the codebase's own established idiom — `ConstellationReveal.kt:152` and `MotionPreferences.kt:51` both animate alpha through a `graphicsLayer` lambda.

The frame pipeline runs at 60 fps either way — a `graphicsLayer` alpha change still calls `onDescendantInvalidated`, still schedules a frame, and the GPU still re-rasterises the damaged region every tick. What the fix actually saves is the CPU display-list *recording* of the rest of the tree: on this screen that is roughly 20-30 trivial nodes (8 `drawLine`s, a rounded rect plus 5 finger lines, ~4 cached-layout text draws, two circles) — tens to low hundreds of microseconds out of a 16.6 ms budget. That is not "measurable battery drain and heat", and it will not be what makes a low-end device drop preview frames; the pulsing animation itself, which is intentional design and unchanged by the fix, is the real power cost. The `Modifier.fillMaxSize()` detail is also a red herring: without a layer the node's size has no bearing on invalidation scope.

Worth fixing for consistency with the existing house pattern, but it is a cleanup, not a user-visible defect.

title: Press ripple on clickable cards paints square corners over the rounded shape

The ripple and hover/focus state layer therefore fill the 16.dp-rounded corners with square ones on press. Route A (minimal, recommended) — insert `.clip(shape)` immediately before `.clickable(...)`, matching the Card's own shape. Requires `import androidx.compose.ui.draw.clip` where absent:
- ResultsScreen.kt:491 -> `modifier = modifier.fillMaxWidth().clip(RoundedCornerShape(16.dp)).clickable(onClick = onClick).semantics(mergeDescendants = true) { contentDescription = cardDesc }`
- ResultsScreen.kt:380 -> `modifier = modifier.fillMaxWidth().clip(RoundedCornerShape(16.dp)).clickable(onClick = onClick).semantics(mergeDescendants = true) { role = Role.Button }`
- HistoryScreen.kt:106 -> `modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth().clip(MaterialTheme.shapes.medium).clickable(onClick = onClick, role = Role.Button).semantics(...)` — MonthCard passes no `shape`, so it inherits `CardDefaults.shape` (= `MaterialTheme.shapes.medium`, 12.dp); use that token rather than hardcoding 12.dp so the two cannot drift.
- DomainDetailScreen.kt:301 -> `modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth().clip(RoundedCornerShape(12.dp)).clickable(onClick = onClick).semantics { role = Role.Button }`

Route B (the auditor's `Card(onClick = ...)` overload) also works — that overload puts the clickable after `.clip(shape)` inside Surface — but note two side effects: (1) it adds `minimumInteractiveComponentSize()` (harmless here, every card exceeds 48.dp); (2) it resolves elevation through `elevation.shadowElevation(enabled, interactionSource)`, so MonthCard's `defaultElevation = 1.dp` will animate to the pressed token on touch — a behavior change, arguably an improvement. First, drop the argument that contiguity is what saves grade(forScore:) from an arbitrary fallback — the fallback is unreachable because ScoringEngineImpl.swift:60 clamps domain scores to 0...100 and the overall is their average; what contiguity actually buys is that the FIRST loop (line 108, iterating an unordered Dictionary) has exactly one matching band, so it cannot return a different grade than Kotlin on a ruleset with overlapping bands. State that reason instead. Second, and more valuable than the port itself: .github/workflows/ci.yml has no Swift step at all — no xcodebuild, no swift test — so a ported validator would only fire at app launch or in a local test run, and would never gate a commit. Add a macOS job running `swift test` in ios/PalmAstroKit (which picks up the new validator plus the existing ParityTests fixtures), and add a Swift test asserting `try Ruleset.loadDefault()` validates, mirroring RulesetTest.kt:124. title: Rendered share cards persist indefinitely in the cache under a single reused filename
evidence: `val file = File(shareDir, "palmastro_share.png")` — a fixed path written on every share (lines 17-22) and exposed through the FileProvider as `${context.packageName}.fileprovider` (line 24-28) with `addFlags(Intent.FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION)` (line 34). Nothing deletes it after the chooser returns; the only cleanup is `WipeManager.deleteShareCache()` (data-room/.../WipeManager.kt:47-50), which runs solely inside `deleteAllData()`. `SettingsViewModel.setRetention(false)` (line 110-112) calls only `wipeManager.deleteAllScanImages()`, so turning retention off leaves the last rendered card — score, grade, interpretation, and action text — sitting in `cacheDir/share/palmastro_share.png`. Because the filename is constant, every share overwrites the same content URI that previously targeted apps were granted read access to.
userImpact: The last reading a user shared — score, grade, and interpretation text — stays in app cache after they disable retention or think they are done, and a previously targeted app holding a live URI grant to the fixed path can read whatever card is written there next.
verifierNote: Core mechanism verified. ShareHelper.kt:19 writes a fixed-name PNG on every share and nothing deletes it: WipeManager.deleteShareCache() is private and called only from deleteAllData(), and ScanImageCleanupWorker.kt:42 scopes its sweep to filesDir/scans, never cacheDir/share. file_paths.xml exposes <cache-path name="share" path="share/"/>, so the content URI is byte-identical across shares and a temporary read grant still held by an earlier share target resolves to whatever card is written next — the exact reason unique per-share filenames are the standard pattern. The lingering plaintext PNG is also a real posture inconsistency for an app that otherwise runs SQLCipher, excludes all domains from backup and device-transfer, and expires raw images at 24h. Severity stays low: cacheDir is app-private (mode 700), excluded from backup, and the leaked content is the user's own reading shared to an app the user chose, so the cross-target read requires a share target that deliberately retains and re-reads the URI. One part of the finding is mis-diagnosed and I dropped it: settings_retention_title is "Keep raw images" / "Images auto-deleted after 24 hours" (strings.xml:103-104), a promise about raw palm photos only, as ScanImageCleanupWorker's PRD 15/27 scoping confirms — so setRetention(false) leaving a rendered card breaks no stated contract, and the proposed setRetention hook would conflate raw media with derived output while fixing nothing about URI reuse.

title: Share card bitmap is allocated and drawn inside the toolbar click handler on the main thread
userImpact: The share icon does not respond for a visible beat — a 2.4 MB bitmap allocation plus a full card draw lands in one frame, so a frame is dropped and the dialog pops in late rather than instantly.
verifierNote: The code matches the evidence exactly. ResultsScreen.kt:89 and DomainDetailScreen.kt:104 are the only two call sites, and both invoke ShareCardRenderer synchronously inside an IconButton onClick lambda, i.e. on the main thread. renderSummaryCard (ShareCardRenderer.kt:64-134) really does allocate a 1080x560 ARGB_8888 bitmap (totalHeight = 120 header + (60 + 4*70 + 40) body + 60 footer = 560 for the standard 4 domains, so 2,419,200 bytes) and then rasterizes it in software: two full-surface drawColor passes, a clipPath, a LinearGradient header fill, and per-domain text plus drawRoundRect. renderDomainDetailCard additionally runs breakText/measureText wrapping (260-274). Android Canvas/Paint are not thread-confined, so the proposed off-main render is safe and is the correct pattern. I could not refute the defect: it is a genuine main-thread rasterization, not a style preference. What I did refute is the severity and the completeness of the fix. There is no StrictMode policy configured (grep over app/src returns nothing), so this is jank, not a crash. The work is single-digit milliseconds of software raster on a mid-tier device, the dialog was going to appear on the next frame regardless, and the realistic worst case is one skipped frame on an infrequent, non-blocking path -- "the share icon does not respond for a visible beat" is not supported, so medium is too high and low is correct. More importantly the fix is a half-fix: in the same flow ShareHelper.share (ResultsScreen.kt:117, DomainDetailScreen.kt:264) runs bitmap.compress(PNG, 100, out) plus a cacheDir file write synchronously inside the dialog's onConfirm lambda, which is tens to hundreds of milliseconds of main-thread work -- strictly worse than the render being flagged. Fixing only the render leaves the larger offender untouched.

title: Two top-app-bar titles use a lighter weight than the other six
evidence: `title = { Text(stringResource(R.string.history_title)) }` — no fontWeight, so it inherits titleLarge's regular weight. JournalScreen.kt:36 is the same. Every other top bar sets a weight: DomainDetailScreen.kt:83, ExplainabilityScreen.kt:65, GuidanceScreen.kt:93, SettingsScreen.kt:70 and LegalViewerScreen.kt:55 all use `fontWeight = FontWeight.SemiBold`; ResultsScreen.kt:83 uses `fontWeight = FontWeight.Bold, color = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.primary`.

Add `fontWeight = FontWeight.SemiBold` to the two unstyled top-bar titles, matching the other five back-navigable screens:
- app/src/main/kotlin/com/palmastro/app/ui/history/HistoryScreen.kt:50 — `title = { Text(stringResource(R.string.history_title), fontWeight = FontWeight.SemiBold) },`
- app/src/main/kotlin/com/palmastro/app/ui/journal/JournalScreen.kt:36 — `title = { Text(stringResource(R.string.journal_title), fontWeight = FontWeight.SemiBold) },`
No import changes are needed in either file: HistoryScreen.kt already imports androidx.compose.ui.text.font.FontWeight at line 24 (used at lines 88, 112, 118, 145, 172) and JournalScreen.kt already imports it at line 16. Leave ResultsScreen.kt:86 (Bold + primary) alone — it is the deliberate root-screen brand title, not a peer of the back-navigable detail bars.

Alternative, preferable if the team wants this to stop recurring: override `titleLarge` with `fontWeight = FontWeight.SemiBold` in `PalmAstroTypography` in app/src/main/kotlin/com/palmastro/app/ui/theme/Theme.kt, so the weight becomes a token rather than per-file discipline. That would make the five existing SemiBold call-site overrides redundant (they could then be deleted) and leave ResultsScreen's Bold as the only intentional deviation. Note this also changes any other titleLarge usage in the app, so grep for `titleLarge` before taking this route.
userImpact: History and Journal headers look lighter and less deliberate than the rest of the app when navigating between screens.
verifierNote: Confirmed after attempting refutation. Theme.kt's PalmAstroTypography deliberately does NOT override titleLarge (its own KDoc states "app bars/titleLarge ... stay stock"), so TopAppBar's default titleTextStyle resolves to the Material 3 baseline titleLarge = 22sp / FontWeight.Normal (W400). A census of all 8 TopAppBar call sites confirms the split: GuidanceScreen.kt:93, SettingsScreen.kt:70, ExplainabilityScreen.kt:65, DomainDetailScreen.kt:83 and LegalViewerScreen.kt:55 pass FontWeight.SemiBold; ResultsScreen.kt:86 passes FontWeight.Bold + primary color; HistoryScreen and JournalScreen pass nothing and render at W400. title: The new type scale is defined but half the screens still spell its numbers by hand
evidence: Theme.kt:129–146 defines titleMedium 16/23, bodyMedium 14/21, bodySmall 13/19, labelMedium 12/17, labelSmall 11/16. Fifteen non-theme call sites re-spell those exact pairs literally instead of using the token — SettingsScreen.kt:138, :205, :284, :303, :318; HistoryScreen.kt:121, :148, :157, :175; GuidanceScreen.kt:269, :333, :360; ExplainabilityScreen.kt:155, :209; OnboardingScreen.kt:370 — while ResultsScreen was not converted at all: 19 `fontSize = N.sp` literals of which only 2 carry any lineHeight (lines 249 and 568). The result is that the same 13sp caption has a 19sp line box in History (HistoryScreen.kt:121, :148) and a font-metric ~15.2sp line box in Results (ResultsScreen.kt:284, :321, :408, :416), and the same 12sp caption is 17sp in History (:157, :175) versus unset in Results (:335, :462, :463, :464).
fix:
Do NOT apply the tokens as the auditor wrote them — titleMedium is SemiBold and labelMedium is Bold + 0.5sp letterSpacing, while most of the literal sites are plain-weight, so a literal swap silently bolds them.

Regressions the proposed fix would cause:
- SettingsScreen.kt:138, :303, :318 are `fontSize = 16.sp, lineHeight = 23.sp` with NO fontWeight. `style = MaterialTheme.typography.titleMedium` would bold every settings row label and the retention title.
- ResultsScreen.kt:462, :463, :464 and HistoryScreen.kt:157 are plain 12sp onSurfaceVariant. `labelMedium` would make them Bold with 0.5sp tracking.
- ResultsScreen.kt:545 is 13sp SemiBold; `bodySmall` is Normal weight.

Correct approach:
1. Split weight out of the size tokens, or spell the delta at the call site. For the plain-weight cases use `style = MaterialTheme.typography.bodySmall` (13sp/19sp, Normal) at ResultsScreen.kt:284, :321, :408, :416 and HistoryScreen.kt:121, :148 — HistoryScreen:121/:148 are Medium weight, so those need `.copy(fontWeight = FontWeight.Medium)` or should stay as-is.
2. There is no plain-weight 12sp token in the scale. Either add one (e.g. `labelLarge`-slot or a new `captionSmall` at 12/17 Normal) in Theme.kt, or write `MaterialTheme.typography.labelMedium.copy(fontWeight = FontWeight.Normal, letterSpacing = 0.sp)` at ResultsScreen.kt:335, :462-464 and HistoryScreen.kt:157. Keep plain `labelMedium` only where the text is already Bold (ResultsScreen.kt:395).
3. For SettingsScreen.kt:138, :303, :318, add a 16/23 Normal-weight token rather than reusing SemiBold titleMedium — or simply leave them, since they already spell the token's metrics and are visually correct.
4. The genuinely load-bearing part of this finding is narrower than stated: ResultsScreen's bare-fontSize captions inherit bodyLarge's 24sp lineHeight. The minimal, zero-regression fix is to add the matching `lineHeight` to the 19 ResultsScreen literals (13.sp -> lineHeight 19.sp, 12.sp -> 17.sp, 11.sp -> 16.sp, 14.sp -> 21.sp, 16.sp -> 23.sp) so Results matches the other screens, and defer the full token migration to a dedicated refactor that also resolves the weight-vs-size token split.
userImpact: Identical captions have different line spacing on Results versus History, so vertical rhythm breaks when a user moves between the two screens — and the next type change has to be made in 100+ places instead of one.

title: VIBRATE is declared in the manifest and genuinely used, but the Play permissions doc omits it and its checklist forbids it
evidence: `<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.VIBRATE" />` — genuinely required, since `HapticPlayer` calls `v.vibrate(effect())` on a real `Vibrator` obtained from `VIBRATOR_MANAGER_SERVICE`/`VIBRATOR_SERVICE` (app/src/main/kotlin/com/palmastro/app/haptics/Haptics.kt:74, 87-93), and the file's own KDoc says "Requires android.permission.VIBRATE in the manifest" (Haptics.kt:33). docs/store/play/permissions.md has sections only for CAMERA (line 9), INTERNET (line 23) and POST_NOTIFICATIONS (line 31), and its pre-submission checklist reads: `- [ ] \`aapt dump permissions\` on the release AAB lists exactly: \`CAMERA\`, \`INTERNET\`, \`POST_NOTIFICATIONS\` ... audit anything unexpected` (lines 71-74).
fix:
In docs/store/play/permissions.md, insert a fourth section after line 36 (before the "## Permissions intentionally NOT used" heading):

### `android.permission.VIBRATE`

- **Why:** Haptic feedback in the scan and reveal flows (capture tick, quality-gate pass/fail, guidance reveal) — `HapticPlayer` in `app/src/main/kotlin/com/palmastro/app/haptics/Haptics.kt`, called from `ScanScreen.kt` and `GuidanceScreen.kt`.
- **Scope:** Short low-amplitude effects only; no-ops when the device has no vibrator or the system touch-feedback setting is off. Collects and transmits nothing. Normal install-time permission — no Play Console declaration form applies.

Then amend the checklist at lines 71-72 to read: `aapt dump permissions` on the release AAB lists exactly: `CAMERA`, `INTERNET`, `POST_NOTIFICATIONS`, `VIBRATE` (plus any OS-implied ones ...).
userImpact: Whoever runs the pre-submission checklist sees an undocumented permission in the release AAB and either blocks the release to investigate, or answers a Play permissions question with a list that does not match the artifact.
verifierNote: Verified end to end and could not refute it. AndroidManifest.xml:8 declares VIBRATE and no flavor/release manifest strips it (only app/ and data-room/ main manifests exist outside build/). The permission is genuinely required: Haptics.kt:74 calls v.vibrate(effect()) on a real Vibrator resolved at lines 87-93, and HapticPlayer is live code invoked from ScanScreen.kt:170,223 and GuidanceScreen.kt:86 — so it cannot be deleted instead. docs/store/play/permissions.md declares itself canonical and sourced from "current app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml" (line 3) but has sections only for CAMERA (9), INTERNET (23), POST_NOTIFICATIONS (31), and its checklist at 71-74 says "lists exactly" those three. The checklist's escape hatch names only OS-implied permissions (RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED/SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM), which does not cover a first-party declaration, so VIBRATE reads as "unexpected" and triggers an investigation. Not documented elsewhere either: grep -rni vibrat across docs/ and the PRD hits only docs/launch/UX_ROADMAP.md:68-70, an implementation roadmap, not the Play store doc. Severity low is right — doc drift with no runtime or user-facing effect. One claimed-impact correction: VIBRATE is a normal install-time permission with no Play Console declaration form, so the "answers a Play permissions question with a mismatched list" half of the impact is overstated; the real cost is a false positive on the pre-submission checklist.
